basis: Typical adult doses as used in UK practice (BNF, Resuscitation Council UK, JBDS, AAGBI/Association of Anaesthetists guidance). A study aid: check your local formulary, protocols and the patient in front of you before giving anything.

drugs.name: Dexmedetomidine
drugs.mechanism: Central α2A agonism in the locus coeruleus reduces noradrenergic output: sedation that resembles natural sleep (rousable, cooperative), sympatholysis and an opioid-sparing effect, with little respiratory depression.

dose.dose: 0.2–1.4 micrograms/kg/h IV infusion, titrated; a 1 microgram/kg loading dose over 10 min is often omitted

drugs.onset: IV: ~15 min to effect; elimination half-life ~2 h
pitfalls: Bradycardia and hypotension; transient hypertension with the loading dose (peripheral α2B vasoconstriction)
Not enough on its own for deep sedation or for paralysed patients
Reduce in hepatic impairment; withdrawal (agitation, hypertension) after prolonged infusion

drugs.name: Propofol
drugs.mechanism: Positive allosteric modulator of the GABA-A receptor, prolonging chloride channel opening; rapid redistribution gives quick, clear-headed recovery.

dose.dose: 1.5–2.5 mg/kg IV, titrated (less in the elderly or haemodynamically unstable)
4–12 mg/kg/h IV, or by target-controlled infusion
0.3–4 mg/kg/h IV

drugs.onset: One arm–brain circulation (~30 s); offset 5–10 min after a bolus
pitfalls: Dose-dependent hypotension and apnoea
Propofol infusion syndrome with prolonged high-dose infusion (> 4 mg/kg/h for > 48 h): metabolic acidosis, rhabdomyolysis, hyperkalaemia, arrhythmia
Lipid emulsion: supports bacterial growth (aseptic handling), raises triglycerides with long infusions
Pain on injection

drugs.name: Ketamine
drugs.mechanism: Non-competitive NMDA receptor antagonism produces dissociative anaesthesia and strong analgesia; indirect sympathomimetic effects usually maintain blood pressure.

dose.dose: 1–2 mg/kg IV (4–10 mg/kg IM)
0.1–0.3 mg/kg IV, titrated

pitfalls: Emergence phenomena (vivid dreams, agitation); a small benzodiazepine dose reduces them
Raises heart rate and blood pressure, but is a direct myocardial depressant when catecholamines are exhausted
Increased secretions; airway reflexes are relatively preserved, not guaranteed

drugs.name: Etomidate
drugs.mechanism: GABA-A positive allosteric modulator with minimal effect on sympathetic tone or myocardial contractility, so it is haemodynamically stable.

dose.dose: 0.2–0.3 mg/kg IV

pitfalls: Adrenocortical suppression (11β-hydroxylase inhibition) for 24 h or more after a single dose; contested in sepsis
Myoclonus, pain on injection, nausea and vomiting

drugs.name: Midazolam
drugs.mechanism: Binds the benzodiazepine site of the GABA-A receptor, increasing the frequency of chloride channel opening: anxiolysis, sedation, amnesia, anticonvulsant effect.

dose.dose: 1–2.5 mg IV, then 1 mg increments to effect (0.5–1 mg in the elderly); usually ≤ 3.5–7.5 mg in total
10 mg buccal or IM

pitfalls: Respiratory depression, especially combined with opioids
The elderly are much more sensitive; titrate slowly
Active metabolite (α-hydroxymidazolam) accumulates in renal failure; CYP3A4 interactions
Reversal: flumazenil

drugs.name: Fentanyl
drugs.mechanism: μ-opioid receptor agonist about 100 times as potent as morphine; highly lipid soluble, so fast onset and, after single doses, short action by redistribution.

dose.dose: 25–50 micrograms IV, titrated (1–2 micrograms/kg)
1–3 micrograms/kg IV at induction

drugs.onset: IV 2–5 min; single dose lasts 30–60 min
pitfalls: Respiratory depression; chest wall rigidity with rapid large doses
Context-sensitive half-time grows with infusion length
CYP3A4 interactions; serotonin toxicity with serotonergic drugs
Reversal: naloxone

drugs.name: Morphine
drugs.mechanism: μ-opioid receptor agonist: supraspinal and spinal analgesia, sedation, respiratory depression, miosis, reduced gut motility.

dose.dose: 1–2 mg IV every 5 min to effect, with monitoring
5–10 mg immediate-release every 4 h as needed

drugs.onset: IV 5–10 min, peak ~20 min; lasts 3–4 h
pitfalls: Morphine-6-glucuronide (active) accumulates in renal impairment: sedation, respiratory depression
Histamine release: hypotension, itch, bronchospasm
Nausea, vomiting, constipation (prescribe a laxative)
Reversal: naloxone

drugs.name: Naloxone
drugs.mechanism: Competitive antagonist at μ (and κ, δ) opioid receptors; displaces opioid agonists.

dose.dose: 400 micrograms IV/IM, repeated every 2–3 min as needed (larger doses for synthetic opioids)
Titrate 20–100 micrograms IV to restore breathing without reversing analgesia

pitfalls: Shorter-acting than many opioids: re-narcotisation, so observe or infuse
Precipitates acute withdrawal in dependent patients
Sympathetic surge: hypertension, arrhythmia, pulmonary oedema

drugs.name: Flumazenil
drugs.mechanism: Competitive antagonist at the benzodiazepine site of the GABA-A receptor.

dose.dose: 200 micrograms IV over 15 s, then 100 micrograms every 60 s as needed; usually ≤ 1 mg in total

pitfalls: Seizures in benzodiazepine-dependent patients or mixed overdoses (e.g. tricyclics); not for undifferentiated coma
Shorter-acting than most benzodiazepines: re-sedation

drugs.name: Rocuronium
drugs.mechanism: Competitive antagonist at post-junctional nicotinic acetylcholine receptors.

dose.dose: 0.6 mg/kg IV
1–1.2 mg/kg IV
0.15 mg/kg IV as needed

drugs.onset: 60–90 s at 0.6 mg/kg (faster at RSI doses); lasts 30–45 min
pitfalls: A leading cause of peri-operative anaphylaxis
No sedation or analgesia: risk of awareness
Prolonged in hepatic impairment and the elderly; monitor with train-of-four
Reversal: sugammadex, or neostigmine with glycopyrronium once recovering

drugs.name: Suxamethonium
drugs.mechanism: Two linked acetylcholine molecules: agonist at nicotinic receptors causing persistent depolarisation (fasciculation, then phase I block); hydrolysed by plasma cholinesterase.

dose.dose: 1–1.5 mg/kg IV

pitfalls: Hyperkalaemia (~0.5 mmol/L rise); dangerous after burns, denervation, crush injury or prolonged immobility (from ~24 h onwards)
Triggers malignant hyperthermia
Bradycardia, especially with repeat doses and in children
Prolonged block with plasma cholinesterase deficiency (suxamethonium apnoea)
Myalgia; raises intra-ocular, intragastric and intracranial pressure

drugs.name: Sugammadex
drugs.mechanism: Encapsulates rocuronium (and vecuronium) one-to-one in plasma, so the drug leaves the neuromuscular junction down its concentration gradient.

dose.dose: 2 mg/kg IV
4 mg/kg IV
16 mg/kg IV

pitfalls: Anaphylaxis; bradycardia
Binds hormonal contraceptives: treat as a missed pill (extra contraception for 7 days)
Does not reverse benzylisoquinoliniums (atracurium, cisatracurium)
Renally excreted; avoid in severe renal impairment
drugs.structureNote: A cyclodextrin ring of eight sugar units: too large for a skeletal card.

drugs.name: Neostigmine
drugs.mechanism: Inhibits acetylcholinesterase, raising acetylcholine at the neuromuscular junction to out-compete a non-depolarising blocker; quaternary, so it does not cross the blood–brain barrier.

dose.dose: 50 micrograms/kg IV (max 5 mg) with glycopyrronium 10 micrograms/kg, once there is spontaneous recovery (train-of-four count ≥ 2–4)

pitfalls: Muscarinic effects (bradycardia to asystole, bronchospasm, secretions, gut motility): always give with an antimuscarinic
Ceiling effect: cannot reverse deep block; excess can itself weaken muscles

drugs.name: Glycopyrronium
drugs.mechanism: Competitive muscarinic antagonist that does not cross the blood–brain barrier: no central effects.

dose.dose: 200–400 micrograms IV
10 micrograms/kg IV (e.g. 0.5 mg with 2.5 mg neostigmine)

pitfalls: Tachycardia, urinary retention, dry mouth
Slower onset than atropine for urgent bradycardia

drugs.name: Atropine
drugs.mechanism: Competitive muscarinic antagonist; crosses the blood–brain barrier.

dose.dose: 500 micrograms IV, repeated every 3–5 min to a maximum of 3 mg
Much larger doses: 1–2 mg IV, doubling every 5 min until the chest is dry

pitfalls: Small doses (< 500 micrograms) can cause paradoxical bradycardia
Central anticholinergic syndrome (confusion, agitation), especially in the elderly
No effect on a denervated (transplanted) heart

drugs.name: Noradrenaline
drugs.mechanism: α1 agonism (vasoconstriction) much greater than β1; raises systemic vascular resistance and MAP.

dose.dose: 0.01–0.5 micrograms/kg/min IV infusion (often higher in refractory shock), titrated to MAP ≥ 65 mmHg

pitfalls: Extravasation causes tissue necrosis (phentolamine); central line preferred, short-term peripheral use only with close monitoring
Reflex bradycardia; peripheral and splanchnic ischaemia
Correct hypovolaemia; concentrations differ between units, so check micrograms/mL

drugs.name: Adrenaline
drugs.mechanism: β1 (inotropy, chronotropy), β2 (bronchodilation, mast cell stabilisation) and α1 (vasoconstriction) agonist.

dose.dose: 500 micrograms IM (0.5 mL of 1 mg/mL, 1:1000) into the anterolateral thigh; repeat after 5 min if no improvement
1 mg IV (10 mL of 0.1 mg/mL, 1:10 000) every 3–5 min
0.01–0.5 micrograms/kg/min IV, titrated

pitfalls: Concentration errors: never give 1 mg/mL (1:1000) as an IV bolus
Tachyarrhythmias, myocardial ischaemia, hyperglycaemia, raised lactate
Anaphylaxis: IM, not subcutaneous

drugs.name: Phenylephrine
drugs.mechanism: Selective α1 agonist: arterial and venous constriction with reflex slowing of the heart.

dose.dose: 50–100 micrograms IV bolus

dose.use: Infusion (e.g. spinal anaesthesia for caesarean section)
dose.dose: 25–100 micrograms/min IV, titrated

pitfalls: Reflex bradycardia; may lower cardiac output in poor LV function
Dilution errors: 10 mg/mL ampoules must be diluted (e.g. to 100 micrograms/mL)

drugs.name: Ephedrine
drugs.mechanism: Mainly indirect (releases noradrenaline from nerve terminals) with some direct α and β agonism: raises heart rate, contractility and blood pressure.

dose.dose: 3–6 mg IV every 3–4 min; usually ≤ 30 mg in total

pitfalls: Tachyphylaxis as noradrenaline stores deplete
Tachycardia; hypertensive crisis with MAO inhibitors
In obstetric spinal hypotension phenylephrine is preferred (less fetal acidosis)

drugs.name: Dobutamine
drugs.mechanism: Racemic: mainly β1 agonism (inotropy) with balanced β2 vasodilation and α1 constriction; raises cardiac output and lowers afterload.

dose.dose: 2.5–10 micrograms/kg/min IV infusion (up to 20), titrated

pitfalls: Tachyarrhythmias and raised myocardial oxygen demand
Hypotension from β2 vasodilation
Tolerance after ~72 h

drugs.name: Vasopressin
drugs.mechanism: V1 receptor agonism causes catecholamine-independent vasoconstriction; V2 effects on the collecting duct (antidiuresis).

dose.dose: 0.01–0.03 units/min IV infusion

pitfalls: Digital, mesenteric and myocardial ischaemia
Hyponatraemia; central line preferred
drugs.structureNote: A nine-amino-acid peptide: shown by name, not structure.

drugs.name: Amiodarone
drugs.class: Class III antiarrhythmic (with class I, II and IV actions)
drugs.mechanism: Blocks potassium channels (prolongs repolarisation and refractoriness) and also sodium and calcium channels and β-adrenoceptors.

dose.dose: 300 mg IV after the third shock; 150 mg after the fifth
300 mg IV over 20–60 min, then 900 mg over 24 h (via a central or large vein)

drugs.onset: IV within hours; elimination half-life ~50 days
pitfalls: Hypotension and bradycardia with IV loading; QT prolongation
Thrombophlebitis peripherally: central line preferred
Long-term: thyroid dysfunction (iodine), pulmonary fibrosis, liver injury, photosensitivity, corneal deposits
Interactions: warfarin, digoxin, simvastatin

drugs.name: Adenosine
drugs.mechanism: A1 receptor agonism at the AV node opens potassium channels and transiently blocks conduction, terminating re-entrant SVT or unmasking atrial activity.

dose.dose: 6 mg rapid IV bolus with a saline flush into a large proximal vein; then 12 mg; a further 12–18 mg per local protocol

pitfalls: Warn the patient: transient asystole, flushing, chest tightness, a sense of doom
Bronchospasm: avoid in asthma
Dangerous in pre-excited AF (WPW)
Start with 3 mg if on dipyridamole, via a central line, or after heart transplant; theophylline and caffeine blunt it

drugs.name: Lidocaine
drugs.class: Amide local anaesthetic; class Ib antiarrhythmic
drugs.mechanism: Blocks voltage-gated sodium channels from inside the cell (use-dependent), stopping action potential propagation.

dose.dose: 3 mg/kg plain (max 200 mg); 7 mg/kg with adrenaline (max 500 mg)
1–1.5 mg/kg IV

drugs.onset: Infiltration 2–5 min, lasts 1–2 h (longer with adrenaline)
pitfalls: Local anaesthetic systemic toxicity: perioral tingling, tinnitus, seizures, arrhythmia, arrest; treat with 20% lipid emulsion (1.5 mL/kg bolus)
Aspirate before injecting; count every source towards the maximum dose

drugs.name: Bupivacaine
drugs.mechanism: Sodium channel blockade, highly protein-bound and lipid-soluble: slow onset, long duration.

dose.dose: 2 mg/kg (max 150 mg), with or without adrenaline
Typically 2–3 mL (10–15 mg)

pitfalls: The most cardiotoxic local anaesthetic: slow dissociation from cardiac sodium channels, VF resistant to treatment; lipid emulsion
Never for IV regional anaesthesia (Bier's block)

drugs.name: Tranexamic acid
drugs.mechanism: Blocks the lysine-binding sites on plasminogen, so plasmin cannot bind and break down fibrin. The drug is the trans isomer.

dose.dose: 1 g IV over 10 min within 3 h of injury, then 1 g over 8 h
1 g IV over 10 min; a second 1 g if bleeding continues after 30 min

pitfalls: In trauma, no benefit (possible harm) after 3 h
Never intrathecal: wrong-route injection causes seizures and death
Reduce in renal impairment; seizures with very high doses

drugs.name: Heparin (unfractionated)
drugs.mechanism: Binds antithrombin and accelerates its inactivation of thrombin (IIa) and factor Xa.

dose.dose: 80 units/kg bolus, then 18 units/kg/h, adjusted to APTT ratio or anti-Xa
5000 units SC every 8–12 h

pitfalls: Heparin-induced thrombocytopenia (5–10 days): check platelets; stop all heparin and use a non-heparin anticoagulant
Bleeding; reversal with protamine (1 mg per 100 units, max 50 mg)
Hyperkalaemia (aldosterone suppression)
drugs.structureNote: A mixture of sulphated polysaccharide chains: shown by name, not structure.

drugs.name: Insulin (soluble)
drugs.mechanism: Activates the insulin receptor tyrosine kinase: GLUT4 glucose uptake, glycogen synthesis, suppressed gluconeogenesis and lipolysis, and potassium shift into cells (Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase).

dose.dose: 0.1 units/kg/h
10 units soluble insulin IV with 25 g glucose; monitor glucose for at least 6 h

pitfalls: Never abbreviate 'units' (a 'U' read as '0' gives a ten-fold overdose); use an insulin syringe
Hypoglycaemia and hypokalaemia: monitor glucose and potassium
drugs.structureNote: A 51-amino-acid peptide in two chains: shown by name, not structure.

drugs.name: Ondansetron
drugs.mechanism: Blocks 5-HT3 receptors on vagal afferents in the gut and in the chemoreceptor trigger zone.

dose.dose: 4 mg IV or oral (up to 8 mg); single IV doses no higher than 16 mg

pitfalls: Dose-dependent QT prolongation
Constipation, headache; serotonin toxicity with serotonergic drugs

drugs.name: Dexamethasone
drugs.mechanism: Glucocorticoid receptor agonist with negligible mineralocorticoid activity: anti-inflammatory, immunosuppressive and antiemetic. 0.75 mg is roughly 5 mg prednisolone.

dose.dose: 4–8 mg IV at induction
10 mg IV every 6 h for 4 days, starting with or before the first antibiotic
10 mg IV, then 4 mg every 6 h

pitfalls: Hyperglycaemia; perineal burning or itching after a rapid IV bolus in an awake patient
Immunosuppression, mood change, adrenal suppression with longer courses

drugs.name: Furosemide
drugs.mechanism: Inhibits the Na⁺/K⁺/2Cl⁻ co-transporter (NKCC2) in the thick ascending limb of the loop of Henle.

dose.dose: 40–80 mg IV slowly (no faster than 4 mg/min)
20–80 mg once daily

drugs.onset: IV 5 min, oral within 1 h; lasts ~6 h
pitfalls: Hypokalaemia, hyponatraemia, hypomagnesaemia, dehydration, AKI
Ototoxicity with rapid high IV doses or aminoglycosides
Gout; sulphonamide sensitivity

drugs.name: Paracetamol
drugs.mechanism: Not fully understood: central COX inhibition where peroxide tone is low, plus serotonergic and cannabinoid (AM404) pathways; little peripheral anti-inflammatory effect.

dose.dose: 1 g oral or IV every 4–6 h, maximum 4 g in 24 h

dose.use: IV, adults < 50 kg or at hepatotoxic risk
dose.dose: 15 mg/kg every 4–6 h, maximum 60 mg/kg in 24 h

pitfalls: Overdose: NAPQI depletes glutathione, causing liver necrosis; treat with acetylcysteine by the nomogram
Reduce for low weight, malnutrition, alcohol excess or liver disease
IV dosing errors (mg vs mL), especially in children

drugs.name: Magnesium sulfate
drugs.class: Electrolyte; NMDA antagonist and calcium channel blocker
drugs.mechanism: Calcium antagonism at voltage-gated channels and NMDA receptor block: anticonvulsant (eclampsia), bronchodilator, antiarrhythmic (torsades).

dose.dose: 4 g IV over 5–15 min, then 1 g/h for 24 h
1.2–2 g IV over 20 min
2 g IV over 10–15 min

pitfalls: Toxicity: loss of tendon reflexes, then respiratory depression and cardiac arrest; monitor reflexes, respiratory rate and urine output
Antidote: calcium gluconate 10 mL of 10% IV
Accumulates in renal impairment; potentiates neuromuscular blockers
drugs.structureNote: An inorganic salt: shown by name, not structure.
